Newly hatched Big skate pups emerge from their egg cases at a total length of approximately 17 centimeters [Lb = approximately 17 centimeters], a modest size that reflects an extended period of yolk-dependent development. This neonatal length represents about seven percent of the species' maximum achievable size, a proportion inferred from comparative data on related rajid species. Upon hatching, these young individuals are immediately capable of benthic foraging, though their small body size likely limits prey selection to small crustaceans and polychaetes during the first few months of life. The initial growth phase is characterized by a steady increase in disc width and body mass, driven by the gradual transition from endogenous to exogenous nutrient sources. Under the thermal conditions typical of their environment, specifically a stable water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the time from egg deposition to hatching spans approximately 365 days [ab = approximately 365 days]. This protracted incubation period is among the longest recorded for skates, consistent with the slow metabolic rates and low ambient temperatures that define the species' developmental physiology. The reliance on maternally provisioned yolk throughout this extended embryonic phase underscores a reproductive strategy that prioritizes offspring size and developmental completeness over rapid production of numerous small young.

As the Big skate progresses through its juvenile and sub-adult stages, it undergoes a gradual but substantial increase in body dimensions, ultimately attaining a maximum recorded total length of 244 centimeters [Li = 244 centimeters]. This ultimate length places Beringraja binoculata among the largest skate species in the North Pacific, with only a few congeners approaching a similar asymptotic size. The pattern of somatic growth follows a decelerating trajectory, with the most rapid increases in length occurring during the early juvenile years before tapering off as the individual approaches sexual maturation. Field surveys and mark-recapture studies indicate that the largest individuals, typically females, may reach this upper size limit after several decades of sustained growth, provided they encounter favorable prey resources and avoid fishing mortality. The ecological implications of such a large body size are considerable: adult Big skates function as apex benthic predators, capable of consuming a wide variety of teleost fishes, cephalopods, and large decapod crustaceans that are inaccessible to smaller elasmobranchs. Additionally, the species' expansive disc provides a large surface area for substrate contact, facilitating efficient foraging on infaunal prey through a combination of suction and excavation behaviors. The morphological shift from a roughly 17-centimeter pup to a 244-centimeter adult represents an order-of-magnitude increase in length and a corresponding exponential increase in body mass, reflecting a life-history strategy that emphasizes slow growth, delayed reproduction, and extreme longevity.

Sexual maturation in the Big skate exhibits a pronounced dimorphism, with females reaching puberty at a significantly larger body size than males. Specifically, the total length at puberty for females is 130 centimeters [Lp = 130 centimeters], whereas males attain puberty at a total length of 105 centimeters [Lp = 105 centimeters]. This size disparity is common among elasmobranchs and is generally attributed to the higher energetic demands of egg production and gestation in females, which require a larger body frame to accommodate developing ova and provide adequate body cavity volume for egg case formation. The onset of gonadal activity in both sexes is correlated with substantial investment in the reproductive organs; in males, testicular recrudescence and clasper calcification mark the transition to a reproductive adult stage, while females initiate the development of functional ovaries and shell glands capable of secreting the characteristic leathery egg cases. These size-based maturity thresholds are derived from extensive field sampling across the species' geographic range, encompassing the Gulf of Alaska, the Bering Sea, and southward along the continental shelf to California. The contrast between the 130-centimeter female and 105-centimeter male maturity lengths highlights a life-history divergence that influences population dynamics, as females must allocate more energy to somatic growth before commencing reproductive activity, thereby lengthening their pre-reproductive period relative to males.

Once a female Big skate reaches sexual maturity at approximately 12 years since birth [tp = approximately 12 years since birth] under the thermal regime of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], she embarks on a reproductive strategy defined by continuous, year-round egg production. Males mature considerably earlier, reaching puberty at roughly 7.5 years since birth [tp = roughly 7.5 years since birth] at the same water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This three-to-four-year gap in maturation timing between the sexes is ecologically significant, ensuring a pool of reproductively active males is consistently available to fertilize newly maturing females as they enter the breeding population. The maximum reproductive output of a gravid female is estimated at approximately 350 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 350 eggs per year], a figure derived from captivity-based observations of continuous oviposition throughout all seasons. This remarkably high fecundity, sustained over the species' long reproductive lifespan, compensates for the extended incubation period and relatively low survivorship of early life stages. Each egg is encased in a tough, amber-colored capsule with distinctive lateral keels and horns, which provides mechanical protection against predators and environmental abrasion during the prolonged embryonic development. The species' ability to reproduce year-round, without a defined spawning season, is a notable adaptation to the relatively stable thermal conditions of the continental shelf environment. The combination of a 130-centimeter female maturity length and the capacity for sustained annual egg production positions the Big skate as a highly fecund yet slow-maturing species, a demographic profile that renders it vulnerable to overfishing.

The maximum known lifespan of the Big skate is approximately 26 years [am = approximately 26 years] in individuals inhabiting waters at 7 °C [T = 7 °C], a figure that aligns with the slow growth rates and late maturity observed in this species. This extraordinary longevity, combined with the continuous egg-laying capability of mature females, results in an extraordinary lifetime reproductive output. Over a reproductive window spanning roughly 14 years (from maturity at age 12 to senescence in the mid-twenties), a single large female may deposit over 4,900 eggs, though natural mortality and environmental variability reduce the effective contribution to the next generation. The ultimate total length of 244 centimeters [Li = 244 centimeters] is thus rarely achieved in the wild, as many individuals succumb to fishing pressure, predation by marine mammals, or age-related physiological decline before reaching this asymptotic size. The species' overall life-history syndrome—characterized by a 17-centimeter birth length, late age at female puberty (12 years), an annual egg production of 350, and a maximum longevity of 26 years—places it at the extreme slow end of the elasmobranch life-history continuum. Comparative analyses with congeners such as Beringraja pulchra reveal similar patterns, though B. binoculata exhibits notably higher fecundity. Conservation assessments must therefore account for the species' low intrinsic population growth rate, which limits its capacity to recover from exploitation even when fishing mortality is reduced, given the protracted time to maturity and the moderate annual egg output relative to total body size.
